newsitem.title: CANADA: TransCanada busy on international front.
newsitem.headline: TransCanada busy on international front.

text.p: TransCanada PipeLines Ltd, serving notice it was serious about international expansion, announced multi-million-dollar projects in Mexico and the United States on Thursday.

TransCanada, the country's biggest pipeline company, said its consortium beat out four other corporate groups in its bid to build and operate a US$250 million-US$300 million natural gas pipeline in Mexico's Yucatan peninsula.

Also on Thursday, 50-percent-owned Great Lakes Gas Transmission, a pipeline that carries Canadian gas through the northern U.S., unveiled plans for a US$2.5 billion expansion project which would double the system's capacity.
The Mexican pipeline, called the Merida project, is just one of several proposals that have been studied by the company for the last three to four years.

Other partners in the Merida plan include InterGen and Corporacion GUTSA. The project was developed to ship gas to power plants owned by Mexico's national electric utility and other industrial customers.
"The importance of this is huge," TransCanada spokesman David Annesley said.
"We've got interests in other projects that we think will be furthered because of this."

TransCanada has made an expression of interest in becoming a natural gas local distrubution company in Mexico City and is looking at various other pipeline projects. It said on Thursday it also planned to open an office in the Mexican capital.
The company is involved in other projects in South America and early this year bought a 10 percent stake in the Paiton coal-fired power plant project in Indonesia.

The aim of its international division is to boost its contribution to corporate net earnings to C$100 million by the year 2000 from the current figure of less than zero, Tony McCallum, Annesley's company spokesman counterpart, said.

The Great Lakes project, part of the TransCanada's major Nexus expansion plans for adding export capacity for Canadian gas production, would increase the capacity of that system by two billion cubic feet per day by the year 2000.

For the total system expansion, which includes TransCanada's mainline, the company has precedent agreements for 1.4 billion cubic feet of new firm capacity, but that could be expanded to 2.3 BCFD, Annesley said.
Of that, about 500 million cubic feet a day off new capacity is expected to be added next year.
TransCanada's partner in Great Lakes is Houston-based Coastal Corp
